{{legend0|#D0D0D0|No election}} }} United States gubernatorial elections were held on November 3, 2009, in the states of [[New Jersey]] and [[Virginia]], as well as in the [[Commonwealth (United States insular area)|U.S. commonwealth]] of the [[Northern Mariana Islands]] on November 7, 2009. Both state governorships were previously held by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] elected in [[2005 United States gubernatorial elections|2005]], and both were won by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] in 2009; the local [[Covenant Party (Northern Mariana Islands)|Covenant Party]] maintained control of the governorship of the Marianas. These elections formed part of the [[2009 United States elections]]. Due to the passage of [[Northern Mariana Islands Senate|Senate]] Legislative Initiative 16–11, this was the last year in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands in which a gubernatorial election occurred on a pre-midterm, [[off-year election]] year, as the next gubernatorial election would be in [[2014 Northern Mariana Islands gubernatorial election|2014]].{{cite news|first=Haidee V. |last=Eugenio |title=CNMI holds first runoff election |url=http://www.saipantribune.com/newsstory.aspx?newsID=95301&cat=1 |work=[[Saipan Tribune]] |date=2009-11-23 |access-date=2009-11-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120112021521/http://www.saipantribune.com/newsstory.aspx?newsID=95301&cat=1 |archive-date=2012-01-12 }}{{cite news|first=Gemma|last=Casas|title=Northern Marianas' election race heats up|url=http://www.radioaustralianews.net.au/stories/200911/2744614.htm?desktop|work=[[Radio Australia]]|date=2009-11-17|access-date=2009-11-23|archive-date=2011-07-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717125217/http://www.radioaustralianews.net.au/stories/200911/2744614.htm?desktop|url-status=usurped}} The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] held 28 governorships, while the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] held 22. In this election, both U.S. governorships up for election were held by Democrats, while the governorship of the Northern Mariana Islands was held by the [[Covenant Party (Northern Mariana Islands)|Covenant Party]]. In New Jersey, incumbent governor [[Jon Corzine]] ran for re-election on a second term, but lost to Republican challenger, former [[United States Attorney for the District of New Jersey]] [[Chris Christie]]. In Virginia, incumbent [[Tim Kaine]], who was term-limited, was succeeded by [[Bob McDonnell]]. This was the last election in which the Democrats held a majority of governorships until [[2026 United States gubernatorial elections|2026]]. ==Election predictions== Several sites and individuals publish predictions of competitive seats. These predictions look at factors such as the strength of the [[incumbent]] (if the incumbent is running for re-election), the strength of the candidates, and the partisan leanings of the state (reflected in part by the state's [[Cook Partisan Voting Index]] rating). The predictions assign ratings to each state, with the rating indicating the predicted advantage that a party has in winning that seat. Most election predictors use: * "tossup": no advantage * "tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean" * "lean": slight advantage * "likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage * "safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory {|class="wikitable sortable" |+ !State ![[Cook Partisan Voting Index|PVI]] ! He was considered vulnerable given a number of recent scandals and low approval ratings.[http://www.newsday.com/news/local/wire/newjersey/ny-bc-nj--e-mails-corzines0531may31,0,7109047.story] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080612054325/http://www.newsday.com/news/local/wire/newjersey/ny-bc-nj--e-mails-corzines0531may31,0,7109047.story|date=June 12, 2008}} Former [[Glen Ridge, New Jersey|Glen Ridge]] Mayor Carl Bergmanson, failed 2008 congressional candidate Roger Bacon, and failed 2008 Senate candidate Jeff Boss also sought the Democratic nomination. Corzine won the Democratic primary on June 2. U.S. Attorney [[Christopher J. Christie|Chris Christie]] was the Republican gubernatorial nominee. Christie defeated former [[Bogota, New Jersey|Bogota]] Mayor [[Steve Lonegan]] and veteran [[New Jersey General Assembly|General Assemblyman]] [[Rick Merkt]] in the Republican primary on June 2. [[Christopher Daggett|Chris Daggett]], who was Commissioner of the [[New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection]] under Governor [[Thomas Kean]] and regional administrator of the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] under President [[Ronald W. Reagan]], ran as an independent. Daggett raised enough money to file for public funds and appear in both debates. On November 3, 2009, Republican Christie unseated Democratic incumbent Governor Corzine. His margin of victory was 49% to 45%. Thus, incumbent governor [[Tim Kaine]] could not stand for re-election. Candidates for the Democratic nomination included [[Terry McAuliffe]], former chairman of the [[Democratic National Committee]] and [[Hillary Clinton]]'s former campaign manager; State Senator [[Creigh Deeds]];{{cite web |url=http://www.charlottesvillenewsplex.tv/news/headlines/33942374.html |title=Deeds Weighs In On Recount Process |publisher=Charlottesvillenewsplex.tv |access-date=2010-04-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090815010624/http://www.charlottesvillenewsplex.tv/news/headlines/33942374.html |archive-date=2009-08-15 |url-status=dead }} and State Delegate [[Brian Moran]].[http://www.newsleader.com/article/20081109/NEWS01/811090337/1002/news01]{{dead link|date=April 2010}} Deeds won the Democratic primary on June 9, 2009, with approximately 49% of the vote, beating out Terry McAliffe with 26% and Brian Moran with 23%.{{cite web|url=https://www.voterinfo.sbe.virginia.gov/election/DATA/2009/B19D959E-A4DD-4C27-BC08-30C8F2FF2F92/Unofficial/2_s.shtml |title=2009 June Democratic Primary Unofficial Results |access-date=June 15, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090618231822/https://www.voterinfo.sbe.virginia.gov/election/DATA/2009/B19D959E-A4DD-4C27-BC08-30C8F2FF2F92/Unofficial/2_s.shtml |archive-date=June 18, 2009 }} The Republican nominee was [[Virginia Attorney General]] [[Bob McDonnell]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Jon Corzine]] ran for a second term against [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Chris Christie]], independent [[Christopher Daggett]], and nine others, in addition to several [[2009 New Jersey gubernatorial election#Candidates|write-in candidates]]. Christie won the election, with about 48.5 percent of the vote, to 44.9 percent for Corzine and 5.8 percent for Daggett.{{cite news |title=Official General Election Results |url=http://www.state.nj.us/state/elections/2009results/09general/09-official-general-election-gov-lt-gov-tallies-120109.pdf |access-date=December 2, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091229055520/http://www.state.nj.us/state/elections/2009results/09general/09-official-general-election-gov-lt-gov-tallies-120109.pdf |archive-date=December 29, 2009 |df=mdy-all }} He assumed office on January 19, 2010. This was the first election to fill the newly created office of [[Lieutenant Governor of New Jersey|lieutenant governor]], with the candidates for governor choosing their running mates. [[Kim Guadagno]], Christie's running mate, became New Jersey's first lieutenant governor. Christie won the largest margin for a non-incumbent Republican since [[1969 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1969]]. He was the first Republican to carry Middlesex and Gloucester counties in a gubernatorial election since [[1985 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1985]].{{cite web|url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2009/11/13/can_the_clinton_coalition_survive_the_age_of_obama_99046.html |title=Can the Clinton Coalition Survive Obama? |publisher=RealClearPolitics |date=2009-11-13 |access-date=2016-10-22}} The 2009 election was the only time since [[1961 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1961]] when [[Bergen County]] did not support the winner of the state's gubernatorial election. Chris Daggett's 5.8% of the vote was the best for a third party in a New Jersey gubernatorial election since [[1913 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1913]]. On April 1, Lonegan released the first attack ad of the 2009 campaign, and released another one on April 19. He accused Christie of ethically dubious awarding of no-bid monitor contracts during his tenure as U.S. attorney, described him as a moderate, and made other allegations.{{cite web |url=http://lonegan.com/site/Viewer.aspx?iid=1233&mname=ArticleGroup&rpid=6052 |title=Steve Lonegan for Governor - Campaign Media |website=lonegan.com |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090519015544/http://lonegan.com/site/Viewer.aspx?iid=1233&mname=ArticleGroup&rpid=6052 |archive-date=19 May 2009 |url-status=dead}} However, on April 24, Christie responded with a new 60 second radio ad noting that Lonegan has lost many elections in his career, including losing by a landslide to [[Steve Rothman]] for Congress in 1998 and finishing fourth (out of seven) in the Republican primary of the [[2005 New Jersey gubernatorial election|2005 New Jersey Governor's race]]. He also claimed that Lonegan's "flat tax" plan, a crucial part of the candidate's platform which calls for applying the same income tax rate to everyone, "would raise taxes on almost 70 percent of New Jersey workers", and characterized Lonegan's previous attacks as "desperate."{{cite web|author=Patti Sapone/The Star-Ledger |url=http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/04/gop_governor_candidate_chris_c.html |title=GOP governor candidate Chris Christie launches radio ads targeting Steve Lonegan |website=NJ.com |date= April 25, 2009|access-date=2016-10-22}} Among those to endorse Christie in the primary were former New Jersey governor [[Thomas Kean]], businessman [[Steve Forbes]], former New York City Mayor [[Rudy Giuliani]] and former Massachusetts governor [[Mitt Romney]].{{cite web|author=Tony Kurdzuk/The Star-Ledger |url=http://www.nj.com/politics/index.ssf/2009/05/mitt_romney_to_endorse_nj_gube.html |title=Mitt Romney to endorse N.J. gubernatorial candidate Chris Christie today |website=NJ.com |date= May 28, 2009|access-date=2016-10-22}} In addition, all county GOP organizations endorsed Christie, as did several New Jersey congressmen. [[Joe the Plumber]] endorsed Lonegan and campaigned with him on May 5.{{cite web|author=Al Goldis |url=http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/04/joe_the_plumber_comes_to_nj_to.html |title='Joe the Plumber' comes to N.J. to support GOP Gov candidate Steve Lonegan |website=NJ.com |date=2009-04-21 |access-date=2016-10-22}} On May 14, [[United States House of Representatives|United States Rep.]] [[Ron Paul]] (R-Texas) sent out an email endorsing Lonegan and asking for donations to Lonegan's campaign. Economists [[Art Laffer]] and [[Peter Schiff]] also endorsed Lonegan, as did [[New Jersey General Assembly]]man [[Michael J. Doherty]]. Christie was declared the winner of the primary, defeating Lonegan by a margin of 55 to 42 percent. Gov candidate, qualifies for public funds |work=[[The Star-Ledger]]| date = July 7, 2009| url = http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/07/nj_independent_candidate_for_g.html| access-date =July 27, 2009}} Both Democratic and Republican leaders took Daggett's campaign seriously. Only a day before the election, the [[New Jersey Democratic State Committee]] admitted to funding political [[robocalls]] in [[Somerset County, New Jersey|Somerset County]] attacking Christie and urging a vote for Daggett. Party chairman [[Joe Cryan]] initially denied the charges until it was revealed that the disclaimer at the end of the call declared it was paid for by "Victory '09, a project of the NJDSC," the abbreviation referring to the state Democratic party. Kevin Roberts, a spokesman for the [[New Jersey Republican State Committee]], attacked Cryan as an "outright liar," adding that "Corzine's party boss knows what we know: Jon Corzine's record is so dreadful that they feel they need to try to trick voters into a second term."{{cite web|url=http://observer.com/2009/11/democrats-admit-paying-for-pro-daggett-call-obama-records-robocall-for-corzine/ |title= Democrats admit paying for pro-Daggett call; Obama records robocall for Corzine|website= [[The New York Observer]]|date=November 2, 2009|access-date=July 1, 2018}} Similarly, state senator [[Marcia Karrow]], a Christie campaign coordinator in [[Hunterdon County, New Jersey|Hunterdon County]], declared that Daggett voters "might as well pull the lever for Corzine."{{cite news |title=Independent Chris Daggett affecting Hunterdon Republicans and Democrats |newspaper=Hunterdon County Democrat |date=October 16, 2009 |url=https://www.nj.com/hunterdon-county-democrat/index.ssf/2009/10/hunterdon_republicans_democrat.html }} On July 15, the New Jersey chapter of a liberal environmental group, the [[Sierra Club]], released a report critical of the Corzine administration's environmental record, with New Jersey Executive Director [[Jeff Tittel]] stating that group believes "this will go down as the worst environmental administration in state history."{{cite news | title=N.J. Sierra Club blasts Gov. Corzine's environmental record |work=[[The Star-Ledger]]| date = July 15, 2009 | url = http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/07/nj_sierra_club_blasts_gov_corz.html | access-date=November 5, 2009}} The state organization formally endorsed Daggett on August 17, its first endorsement of an independent candidate.{{cite news |title=Sierra Club backs independent for governor |author=Adrienne Lu |newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=August 18, 2009 |url=http://www.philly.com/philly/news/local/20090818_Sierra_Club_backs_independent_for_governor.html }} Corzine was the target of a vigorous advertising campaign funded by the Christie campaign and the [[Republican Governors Association]], attacking his record as governor, tying him to corrupt officials, and assailing him for failing to deliver on his campaign promises. The RGA set up a mock newspaper website, [http://www.corzinetimes.com "The Corzine Times"], collecting newspaper articles critical of Corzine. One of Corzine's main lines of attack involved Christie's ties to the unpopular former president [[George W. Bush]], who appointed Christie to the U.S. Attorney's office in 2001. In August 2009, Bush political strategist [[Karl Rove]] revealed that he had held conversations with Christie about a potential gubernatorial run during Christie's time as U.S. Attorney. U.S. Attorneys are prohibited from engaging in partisan political activities by the [[Hatch Act of 1939]].{{cite news|title=Karl Rove and Chris Christie discussed N.J. governor run while serving as U.S. Attorney|work=[[The Star-Ledger]]|date=August 12, 2009|url=http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/08/karl_rove_says_gop_candidate_c.html|access-date=August 14, 2009|first=Claire|last=Heininger}} Corzine quickly incorporated this into his advertisements targeting Christie.[http://www.politickernj.com/editor/32239/christie-rove-and-us-attorneys-office]{{dead link|date=October 2016}} The Corzine campaign filed requests under the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]] since March 2009 seeking records of budgets, travel expenses, and no-bid contracts from Christie's tenure as U.S. Attorney.{{cite web |title=Corzine wants Christie to join in FOIA requests |url=https://observer.com/2009/10/corzine-wants-christie-to-join-in-foia-requests/ |website=Observer |access-date=8 September 2021 |date=22 October 2009}} The U.S. Attorney's office did not release the requested documents before election day.{{cite web |title=Records relating to FOIA requests, ultimately abandoned, submitted to the Executive Office of U.S. Attorneys from the campaign office of Jon Corzine relating to the service of opponent candidate Chris Christie as U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey, 2009 |url=https://www.governmentattic.org/6docs/DOJ-CorzineFOIAs_2009.pdf |access-date=8 September 2021}} State Sen. [[Loretta Weinberg]] demanded an end to the "logjam" by the U.S. Attorney's office.{{cite web |last1=Pizarro |first1=Max |title=Weinberg demands transparency from Christie |url=https://observer.com/2009/08/weinberg-demands-transparency-from-christie/ |website=Observer |access-date=8 September 2021 |date=7 August 2009}} On August 12, Christie's successor, acting U.S. attorney [[Ralph J. Marra, Jr.]], issued a press release defending the office: {{blockquote|The U.S. Attorney's Office has worked as professionally and expeditiously as it can to fulfill all the requests and has been in virtually daily contact with the Executive Office for United States Attorneys (EOUSA) in Washington to accomplish this burdensome and continuous task. ... At absolutely no time has there been an effort to slow down or inhibit the FOIA process.{{cite web|author=Max Pizarro |url=http://www.politickernj.com/max/32261/marra-defends-his-offices-response-corzine-campaigns-foia-requests |title=Marra defends his office's response to Corzine campaign's FOIA requests | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-08-12 |access-date=2016-10-22}}}} On August 18, 2009, Christie acknowledged that he had loaned $46,000 to First Assistant U.S. Attorney for New Jersey [[Michele Brown (New Jersey official)|Michele Brown]] two years ago, while serving as her superior as the state's U.S. attorney, and that he had failed to report the loan on either his [[Tax return (United States)|income tax returns]] or his mandatory financial disclosure report to the New Jersey Election Law Enforcement Commission.{{cite news | last = Margolin | first = Josh | title = Federal prosecutor who took loan from GOP governor candidate Chris Christie resigns | newspaper= NJ.com | date = August 25, 2009 | url = http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/08/us_prosecutor_at_center_of_chr.html }} In response to the disclosure of the financial relationship between Christie and Brown, Weinberg called on Brown to recuse herself from the task of retrieving U.S. Attorney's Office records requested by the Corzine campaign under the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]].{{cite news | last = Friedman | first = Matt | title = Weinberg wants Brown to recuse herself from FOIA retrievals | newspaper= PolitickerNJ.com | date = August 21, 2009 | url = http://www.politickernj.com/matt-friedman/32503/weinberg-wants-brown-recuse-herself-foia-retrievals }} On August 25, Brown resigned from her post, stating that she does not want to be "a distraction" for the office. Although the Corzine campaign sought to make the loan a major campaign issue, a [[Quinnipiac University Polling Institute|Quinnipiac]] poll showed that only 43% of voters believed that the loan controversy was a legitimate attack, while a [[Plurality (voting)|plurality]] of 49% called it an unfair attack.{{cite news | last = Edge | first = Wally | title = Voters split on Brown & Katz as campaign issues | newspaper= PolitickerNJ.com | date = September 1, 2009 | url = http://www.politickernj.com/wallye/32782/voters-split-brown-katz-campaign-issues }} As of September 20, Corzine had put out 4,806 television advertisements to Christie's 1,393 ads.{{cite magazine |url=http://realclearpolitics.blogs.time.com/2009/10/08/ad-wars-in-nj-va-and-nyc/ |title=Ad Wars in NJ, VA, and NYC - Real Clear Politics – TIME.com |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091008204930/http://realclearpolitics.blogs.time.com/2009/10/08/ad-wars-in-nj-va-and-nyc/ |archive-date=8 October 2009 |url-status=dead}} ===Debates=== Corzine, Christie, and Daggett debated each other three times by the election. Two debates were sanctioned by the state's Election Law Enforcement Commission; Christie and Daggett were required to participate in these debates, as they received public financing. Corzine did not seek public financing but appeared in both ELEC debates. The first debate, sanctioned by the ELEC and sponsored by [[New Jersey Network|NJN]], [[Gannett]] New Jersey, and ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'', was held on October 1 in [[Trenton, New Jersey|Trenton]]. It was televised on NJN.{{cite web|url=http://www.politickernj.com/wallye/32846/final-debate-schedule |title=Final debate schedule | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-09-02 |access-date=2016-10-22}} It was widely reported by mainstream media that Chris Daggett won the first debate.{{cite web|url=http://njelection.wordpress.com/2009/10/12/daggett-wins-election-debate/ |title=Daggett Wins Election Debate | NJ Election 2009 - Chris Daggett and Election Candidates |website=Njelection.wordpress.com |date= October 12, 2009|access-date=2016-10-22}} The second ELEC-sanctioned debate, sponsored by [[Fox News]], ''[[The Record (Bergen County)|The Record]]'', [[WWOR-TV]] out of [[Secaucus, New Jersey|Secaucus]], and [[WTXF-TV]] out of [[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania, was held on October 16 at [[William Paterson University]] in [[Wayne, New Jersey|Wayne]]. It was televised on WWOR-TV and WTXF-TV.{{cite web |url=http://www.politickernj.com/max/34181/gubernatorial-candidates-battle-wayne |title=Gubernatorial candidates battle in final TV debate | Politicker NJ | New Jersey Politics News, Reaction, and Analysis |website=www.politickernj.com |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091019232324/http://www.politickernj.com/max/34181/gubernatorial-candidates-battle-wayne |archive-date=19 October 2009 |url-status=dead}} All three candidates appeared in a third debate, which was not sanctioned by the ELEC, that was held on October 22. The debate was broadcast on the radio on [[WBGO]], a [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]]-based jazz station, and was simulcast on [[WNYC]] out of New York City, [[WHYY-FM]] out of Philadelphia, and public radio stations throughout the state of New Jersey.{{cite web|author=Matt Friedman |url=http://www.politickernj.com/matt-friedman/33505/christie-accepts-wbgo-debate |title=Christie accepts WBGO debate | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-09-28 |access-date=2016-10-22}} Christie and Daggett agreed to participate in a fourth debate, broadcast on the radio on [[WKXW|New Jersey 101.5]]; Corzine declined to participate.{{cite web|url=http://www.politickernj.com/editor/33227/corzine-declines-nj-1015-debate |title=Corzine declines NJ 101.5 debate | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-09-17 |access-date=2016-10-22}} === Lieutenant governor factor === {{Main|Lieutenant Governor of New Jersey}} This was the first gubernatorial election since the position of [[Lieutenant Governor of New Jersey|lieutenant governor]] was created{{cite news|title=New lieutenant governor slot is a plum for rising stars|publisher=NJ.com|date=June 15, 2008|url=http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2008/06/new_lieutenant_governor_slot_i.html|access-date=February 7, 2009|first=Claire|last=Heininger}} and the candidates were the first gubernatorial candidates in New Jersey history to pick running mates.{{cite web|author=Mel Evans |url=http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2009/05/gubernatorial_candidates_to_pi.html |title=Gubernatorial candidates to pick lieutenant governor running mates for first time in NJ history |website=NJ.com |date=2009-05-30 |access-date=2016-10-22}} All twelve candidates on the ballot selected their running mates by the July 27, 2009 deadline.[http://www.njelections.org/09results/09general/09-unofficial-general-election-gov-lt-gov-candidates.pdf]{{dead link|date=October 2016}} Christie, as the Republican nominee for governor, selected [[Kim Guadagno]], the sheriff of [[Monmouth County, New Jersey|Monmouth County]]. Others mentioned for the post had included former congressman [[Bob Franks]], [[New Jersey Senate|State Senators]] [[Diane Allen]] and [[Jennifer Beck]], and [[Bergen County, New Jersey|Bergen County]] Clerk [[Kathleen Donovan]]. Corzine, as the Democratic nominee, selected State Senator [[Loretta Weinberg]]. Other mentioned for the post had included Newark Mayor and future U.S. senator [[Cory Booker]], New Jersey senators [[Nia Gill]] and [[Barbara Buono]], New Jersey General Assemblywoman [[Bonnie Watson Coleman]], and wealthy businessman [[Randal Pinkett]]. Daggett, having qualified for matching funds, selected [[Ocean Township, Monmouth County, New Jersey|Ocean Township]]'s [[Frank J. Esposito]], a longtime professor and administrator at [[Kean University]] who served as an advisor to the [[New Jersey Department of Education|Commissioner of Education]] in the [[Thomas Kean]] administration, as his running mate. Others mentioned for the post had included [[Edison, New Jersey|Edison]] Mayor [[Jun Choi]] and [[Passaic County, New Jersey|Passaic County]] freeholder James Gallagher. There was also a debate between the three major candidates for lieutenant governor: [[Loretta Weinberg]], [[Kim Guadagno]], and [[Frank J. Esposito|Frank Esposito]]. This debate, sponsored by Leadership New Jersey, was held at [[Monmouth University]] in [[West Long Branch, New Jersey|West Long Branch]] on October 8. It was televised on [[News 12 New Jersey]] and broadcast on the radio on New Jersey 101.5. === Regional factors === In New Jersey, Republicans tend to be strongest in the Northwest and Shore regions of the state, Democrats tend to be strongest in urban areas, and suburban areas such as those in [[Mercer County, New Jersey|Mercer County]], [[Middlesex County, New Jersey|Middlesex County]], [[Union County, New Jersey|Union County]], [[Passaic County, New Jersey|Passaic County]], and [[Bergen County, New Jersey|Bergen County]] are considered toss-ups. In the Democratic primary, Corzine got over 70% of the vote only in the urban areas, doing relatively poorly among suburban Democrats. His weakest performance was in [[Warren County, New Jersey|Warren County]], where he won with just 55% of the vote.{{cite web|url=http://www.politickernj.com/jeffmichaels/30336/governors-suburban-challenge |title=The Governor's Suburban Challenge | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-06-04 |access-date=2016-10-22}} On the other hand, Corzine performed strongly in [[Bergen County]], winning with almost 87% of the vote.{{cite web |url=http://www.co.bergen.nj.us/countyclerk/2009%20primary/summary%20report.pdf |title=Archived copy |website=www.co.bergen.nj.us |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091123010015/http://www.co.bergen.nj.us/countyclerk/2009%20primary/summary%20report.pdf |archive-date=23 November 2009 |url-status=dead}} In the Republican primary, Christie lost some key Republican strongholds, such as [[Hunterdon County]] (where he received 45.8%[http://www.co.hunterdon.nj.us/countyclerk/election/unofficialprimary2009.htm]{{dead link|date=October 2016}}) and [[Warren County, New Jersey|Warren County]] (where he received 46.9%{{cite web |url=http://www.co.warren.nj.us/Elections/includings/2009_June_Primary_final.pdf |title=PRIMARY ELECTION JUNE 2, 2009, WARREN COUNTY |website=Co.warren.nj.us |access-date=2016-10-22 |archive-date=November 17, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091117063902/http://www.co.warren.nj.us/Elections/includings/2009_June_Primary_final.pdf |url-status=dead }}) to Lonegan. According to a September 1 [[Quinnipiac University Polling Institute|Quinnipiac University]] poll, [[Hudson County, New Jersey|Hudson County]] and [[Essex County, New Jersey|Essex County]] were the only counties where a majority of voters viewed Corzine favorably. Corzine had upside-down ratings in all 19 other counties in that poll.{{cite web|url=http://www.politickernj.com/wallye/32773/how-quinnipiac-makes-upside-down-jon-cake |title=How Quinnipiac makes the Upside-Down Jon cake | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-09-01 |access-date=2016-10-22}} In contrast, Christie had upside-down ratings in those two counties but was viewed favorably by pluralities of voters in every other county except for [[Atlantic County, New Jersey|Atlantic County]], [[Ocean County, New Jersey|Ocean County]], and [[Monmouth County, New Jersey|Monmouth County]], where a majority of voters viewed him favorably. === Political factors === Taxes and the economy were overwhelmingly the top issues in this campaign. Corzine's strongest issue was on education, but it was the most important issue for only 4% of likely voters.{{cite web|author=Alan Steinberg |url=http://www.politickernj.com/alan-steinberg/30521/governors-race-eight-key-quinnipiac-findings |title=Governor's Race: Eight Key Quinnipiac Findings | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-06-11 |access-date=2016-10-22}} Christie attacked Corzine's record of raising taxes, failing to deliver property tax relief, and presiding over a period of unusually high unemployment in the state. Corzine pointed to the global economic recession as the reason for the state's economic troubles. Republicans contended that Corzine's policies led to over-taxation and economic decline, causing an out-migration of residents documented in a report by the [[Edward J. Bloustein School of Planning and Public Policy]] at Rutgers University.{{cite web |url=http://www.nj.com/news/times/regional/index.ssf?/base/news-18/125541271525840.xml&coll=5 |title=The Times of Trenton |website=NJ.com |access-date=2016-10-22 |archive-date=June 5, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605175840/http://www.nj.com/news/times/regional/index.ssf?/base/news-18/125541271525840.xml&coll=5 |url-status=dead }} Christie also campaigned on the issues of ethics, reducing corruption, and ending fiscal waste. These issues were brought back to the forefront of the debate after 44 individuals, including several public officials in New Jersey, were arrested by the FBI in July 2009 in [[Operation Bid Rig]]. Corzine was not a target of the probe; however, the office of a member of his cabinet, [[New Jersey Department of Community Affairs|Commissioner of Community Affairs]] [[Joseph Doria]], was raided by the FBI in connection with Operation Bid Rig. Governor Corzine asked for, and accepted, Doria's resignation on July 23. Doria has not been charged with any crime. Although Corzine has not been accused of any wrongdoing, the corruption sting, which resulted in the arrests of mostly Democratic officials, nevertheless further injured Corzine's reputation. Former [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] Regional Administrator [[Alan J. Steinberg]] predicted in his July 23 column that the corruption scandal would doom Corzine's re-election bid, as ethics would become a major issue again, thus helping Christie.{{cite web|author=Alan Steinberg |url=http://www.politickernj.com/alan-steinberg/31680/corzine-not-corrupt-corruption-scandal-dooms-his-campaign |title=Corzine is Not Corrupt – But The Corruption Scandal Dooms His Campaign | Observer |website=Politickernj.com |date=2009-07-23 |access-date=2016-10-22}} State Senator [[Ray Lesniak]], a prominent Democrat, acknowledged that "If it's about ethics, Corzine loses. Not because Jon Corzine's weak on ethics, but because it's Chris Christie's strength, and now it's national news."{{cite news|title=Corruption Case a Blow to Corzine's Campaign|work=The New York Times|date=July 24, 2009|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/07/25/nyregion/25jersey.html?_r=1&ref=nyregion|access-date=July 28, 2009|first=David M.|last=Halbfinger}} Under normal circumstances, Corzine would have been considered to have an inherent advantage in the "[[blue state]]" of New Jersey. No Republican has won New Jersey's electoral votes in a presidential election since [[George H. W. Bush]] in [[1988 United States presidential election|1988]]. Prior to the 2009 election, no Republican had won a statewide election in New Jersey since [[1997 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1997]], when Governor [[Christine Todd Whitman]] won re-election with 47.1% of the vote. The last Republican to win a statewide election in New Jersey with over 50% of the vote was incumbent governor [[Thomas Kean]] in 1985, who won with 71% of the vote.Sullivan, Joseph F. [https://select.nytimes.com/search/restricted/article?res=F50711FC3B590C7A8CDDA80994DE484D81 "Shapiro Criticizes Party for Defeat"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', November 9, 1986. Accessed October 10, 2007. No Republican has won a U.S. Senate election in New Jersey since liberal Republican [[Clifford Case]] in 1972. Between February 2009 and the end of his term, Corzine's approval ratings ranged between 33% and 42%. His disapproval ratings ranged between 46% and 66%.{{cite web|url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/epolls/2009/governor/nj/new_jersey_governor_corzine_job_approval-1090.html |title=Election 2009 - New Jersey Governor - Corzine Job Approval |publisher=RealClearPolitics |access-date=2016-10-22}} These weak poll numbers were the result of several factors. Going into the 2009 fiscal year, New Jersey faced a budget shortfall of approximately $3 billion. Corzine attempted to close this gap by enacting pay freezes and furloughs of state employees, a policy that was unpopular with many public employee unions, a major Democratic constituency. Corzine had also cut state aid to local governments, which hurt his standing in the urban areas which made up another key segment of the Democrats' base. Across the state, voters expressed sentiments that taxes were too high and too few budget cuts were being made, and further public dissatisfaction mounted following the [[Great Recession|economic recession in 2008]]. By the end of May 2009, Corzine's job approval was the lowest of any New Jersey governor in modern history, putting him behind Christie in early election polling.{{cite web|url=http://www.governing.com/topics/politics/The-Corzine-Chase.html|title=The Corzine Chase|website=Governing |date=2009-05-31 |access-date=2018-07-01}} These weak numbers indicated that he could be vulnerable against a strong Republican challenger.{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2009/jun/16/nj-gop-eager-to-oust-corzine-as-ratings-slump/|title=N.J. GOP sees Corzine as vulnerable |website=The Washington Times |date=2009-06-16 |access-date=2018-07-01}} Moreover, no Democrat has won re-election to the state governor's office since [[Brendan Byrne]]'s victory in [[1977 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1977]].{{cite web|url=https://www.insidernj.com/one-term-and-done-the-curse-that-the-next-dem-governor-would-face/ |title=One-Term and Done: The Curse that the Next Dem Governor Would Face |website=Insider NJ |date=2017-02-28 |access-date=2018-07-01}} Some thought that Corzine would benefit from the popularity of President [[Barack Obama]], who carried the state in 2008 with 57% of the vote and had higher approval ratings than Corzine had. However, Obama's approval ratings in the state varied, ranging from as high as 68% in a June [[Quinnipiac University Polling Institute|Quinnipiac]] poll{{cite web |url=http://www.quinnipiac.edu/x1284.xml?ReleaseID=1312&What=&strArea=;&strTime=120 |title=Pre-Medical Studies Program |website=Quinnipiac.edu |access-date=2016-10-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090619064449/http://www.quinnipiac.edu/x1284.xml?ReleaseID=1312&What=&strArea=;&strTime=120 |archive-date=June 19, 2009 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }} to as low as 53% in a PPP poll, which is lower than what he obtained on election day in 2008.[http://www.publicpolicypolling.com/pdf/PPP_Release_NJ_701.pdf]{{dead link|date=October 2016}} Another poll in July gave him 55% approval in the state, also less than what he obtained on election day. In the same poll 47% believed Obama would help Corzine's numbers in the election by campaigning with him.{{cite web|url=http://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/politics/elections2/election_2009/new_jersey/election_2009_new_jersey_governor/ |title=Election 2009: New Jersey Governor - Rasmussen Reports |website=Rasmussenreports.com |date=2009-10-30 |access-date=2016-10-22}} After Vice President Biden's June appearance at a "poorly attended" Corzine primary-night event, the [[Barack Obama administration]] approached [[President of the New Jersey Senate]] and former governor [[Richard Codey]] to consider running in the governor's place if the incumbent withdrew from his reelection bid, citing polls showing that Codey led Christie.Margolin, Joshua. "[http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2009/11/democratic_leaders_nearly_aban.html Gov. Corzine's N.J. re-election bid nearly abandoned as White House concerns grew]" ''The Star-Ledger'', November 4, 2009. Obama held a campaign rally for Corzine on July 16. The election was held concurrently with other elections for [[2009 Virginia elections|Virginia's statewide offices]], the [[2009 Virginia House of Delegates election|House of Delegates]], and other [[2009 United States elections|United States offices]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Tim Kaine]] was ineligible to run for re-election, as the [[Constitution of Virginia]] prohibits its governors from serving consecutive terms. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Bob McDonnell]] was elected as [[Governor of Virginia|governor]] as part of a Republican sweep. Republican [[Bill Bolling]] was reelected as [[Lieutenant Governor of Virginia|lieutenant governor]], and Republican [[Ken Cuccinelli]] was elected as [[Attorney General of Virginia|attorney general]]. The winners were inaugurated on January 16, 2010, and served until January 11, 2014. [[Senate of Virginia|State Senator]] [[Creigh Deeds]] was selected as the Democratic nominee, having defeated former [[Democratic National Committee]] Chair [[Terry McAuliffe]] and former [[Virginia House of Delegates|state Delegate]] [[Brian Moran]] in the Democratic [[Partisan primary|primary election]].{{cite news |url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/01/03/AR2009010301679.html |title= Former DNC Chairman McAuliffe Announces Run for Va. Governor |first= Amy |last= Gardner |newspaper=The Washington Post |date= January 3, 2009 |access-date=January 3, 2009}}{{cite web |url=https://www.voterinfo.sbe.virginia.gov/election/DATA/2009/B19D959E-A4DD-4C27-BC08-30C8F2FF2F92/Unofficial/2_s.shtml |title=2009 June Democratic Primary Unofficial Results |website=Virginia State Board of Elections |access-date=2009-06-15 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090618231822/https://www.voterinfo.sbe.virginia.gov/election/DATA/2009/B19D959E-A4DD-4C27-BC08-30C8F2FF2F92/Unofficial/2_s.shtml |archive-date=June 18, 2009 |df=mdy-all }} This was the first contested Democratic primary in two decades.{{cite news|last=Kumar|first=Anita|date=December 2, 2008|title=Gubernatorial Candidates Square Off|newspaper=The Washington Post|url=http://voices.washingtonpost.com/virginiapolitics/2008/12/post_121.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120612031553/http://voices.washingtonpost.com/virginiapolitics/2008/12/post_121.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 12, 2012|access-date=December 2, 2008}} McDonnell, a former state attorney general, was selected at his party's nominating [[Political convention|convention]].{{cite news |url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/11/07/AR2008110703306.html |title= Clear Path to Governor's Race |first= Anita |last= Kumar |newspaper=The Washington Post |date= November 8, 2008 |access-date=January 6, 2008}} The two major candidates competed in the 2005 Virginia attorney general election, and were in a rematch, but in the Governor's race. McDonnell defeated Deeds in the general election by a margin of 59%–41%, much larger than in the [[2005 Virginia Attorney General election|previous attorney general election]]. This was the last time until [[2021 Virginia elections|2021]] that a Republican won any statewide election in Virginia. This is also the last time any of the following counties have voted Republican in a statewide race: [[Albemarle County, Virginia|Albemarle]], [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax]], [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William]], [[Henrico County, Virginia|Henrico]], [[Sussex County, Virginia|Sussex]], [[Brunswick County, Virginia|Brunswick]], and the independent city of [[Suffolk, Virginia|Suffolk]]. [[Virginia House of Delegates|State Delegate]] [[Brian Moran]], brother of [[United States House of Representatives|Congressman]] [[Jim Moran]], joined Deeds on January 4, 2008, when he established a [[political action committee]]. For the following year (before McAuliffe indicated his intentions to run), Deeds and Moran picked up endorsements and raised money. On January 3, 2009, [[McLean, Virginia|McLean]] resident [[Terry McAuliffe]], former chairman of the [[Democratic National Committee]] and chairman of [[Hillary Clinton]]'s [[Hillary Clinton presidential campaign, 2008|2008 presidential campaign]] announced that he was also running. The Democratic primary, which took place on June 9, 2009, was the first contested in over twenty years.[[File:Primary voting sign (Alexandria).jpg|thumb|250px|Sign outside Alexandria City Hall, indicating the nearest polling place]] Moran received many endorsements from members of the [[Democratic Party of Virginia|State Democratic Party]] as well as the mayors of the [[Hampton Roads]] area.{{Citation needed|date=May 2009}} Deeds picked up support from Northern and Western Virginia, such as the endorsement from U.S. Congressman [[Rick Boucher]]. The area of strength for Deeds was concentrated in Western and Southern Virginia, and the area of strength for Moran consisted mostly of Eastern Virginia, with both reaching out to Northern Virginian voters.{{Citation needed|date=May 2009}} The race was close from the beginning, with McAuliffe considered to be a semi-frontrunner due to his lead in the polls and big campaign war chest. However, in the last few weeks of the race, Deeds began to surge in the polls. By election night, June 9, he swept to victory. Deeds spent $14.49 for each vote on the Democratic primary election.
